What a screen's scripts and callbacks talk to: the variables the host put there, the callbacks it registered by name, and the tree itself, which can be looked through by id.

Every element in the tree is named: one that a script gave an id keeps it, and one that was given none has an id made up for it when the context is built, so `getElementById` can reach anything whether or not whoever wrote the script thought to name it.

Every string the tree shows is read through `resolve`, so ${name} anywhere in it is the variable of that name as it stands this frame. Putting a variable here is what makes the screen say something new: nothing else has to be told.

It can also remember what the user did to the tree, by `rememberState` and `restoreState`. Nothing calls those on its own: a screen opening or closing keeps nothing unless the host asks it to.

```java
import net.tutla.craftytml.client.dom.DOMContext;
```

## Members

### `public DOMContext(DOMTreeElement element)`

### `public void putCallBack(String name, Consumer<CTMLCallback> consumer)`

### `public void putVariable(String name, Object value)`

Puts a variable there and tells the screen, so every string that names it is read again and whatever it was showing changes with it. This is the door: the map behind it is this context's own, since a value changed behind the screen's back is one nothing would redraw for.

### `public void removeVariable(String name)`

Takes a variable away, which leaves every string that named it reading as empty.

### `public Object getVariableValue(String name)`

### `public Map<String, Object> getVariables()`

### `public String resolve(String raw)`

Reads a string the way the screen shows it: ${name} is the variable of that name, and one nothing has put there yet reads as nothing at all rather than leaving the braces on show. $${ is how a string says ${ and means it. A string with no ${ in it is handed straight back, which is almost every string there is.

### `public static boolean hasVariables(String raw)`

Whether a string has anything in it for `resolve` to do.

### `public void refresh()`

Says that every string naming a variable is out of date: the ones that are text are laid out again, and the ones that are class lists are read onto their elements afresh. Only the elements carrying a ${ are touched, so a variable nothing mentions costs a walk and no layout.

### `public boolean fire(CallbackType type, DOMTreeElement element, int keycode)`

Calls the callback the element names, if it names one and the host registered it under that name. Says whether anything was actually called, so whatever is handling the press knows to swallow it.

### `public DOMTreeElement getElementById(String id)`

The element with this id anywhere under the head node, or null where nothing has it.

### `public int rememberState(String key)`

Remembers where this tree's elements were left, under whatever key the host wants them back by. Hands back how many were worth remembering, and forgets the key entirely when none were. Elements are recognised by their ids, so one the script named is found again whatever happens to the tree, while a made up id lasts only as long as the tree that was handed it does.

### `public int restoreState(String key)`

Puts back whatever was remembered under this key, and says how many elements it reached.

### `public static void forgetState(String key)`

Drops what was remembered under a key, so the next restore of it does nothing.
